problem_motivation.content: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) cannot be used as common structural materials due to inherent drawbacks in processing and machining operations.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations.

problem_motivation.content: Refractory high-entropy alloys are difficult to process using traditional methods due to high melting temperatures and hardness, creating a need for additive manufacturing approaches.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Refractory HEAs are particularly difficult to process due to their high melting temperature, high hardness, natural tendency to oxidize and toughness in machining operations [ [12] ]. Hence, there is great interest in finding ways to produce these alloys by additive manufacturing (AM) technologies

problem_motivation.content: The main challenge for synthesizing WTaMoNbV via AM is selecting proper process parameters due to significant diversity in the thermal and physical properties of the alloying elements, particularly their differing melting temperatures and densities.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The main challenge related to the composition of the HEA WTaMoNbV that was selected mainly due to the high melting temperature of its elemental ingredients relates to proper selection of the AM process parameters that can adequately synthesize this alloy. This challenge is mainly due to the significant diversity in the thermal and physical properties of the alloying elements

prior_approach.content: HEA powder was previously produced using conventional arc melting furnaces followed by gas atomization.
prior_approach.evidence_span: So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process.

prior_approach.content: Initial attempts to produce HEAs via AM used mixes of elemental alloying powders for systems like Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5, NbMoTaW, and AlCoFeNiSmTiVZr.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In parallel, some initial AM efforts were dedicated to attempting to produce HEA from a mix of elemental alloying powder composed of the following material systems: Al0.5CrMoNbTa0.5 [ [34] , [35] ], NbMoTaW [ [8] ] and AlCoFeNiSmTiVZr [ [1] ].

prior_approach.content: Senkov et al. successfully produced the WTaMoNbV alloy using conventional vacuum arc melting furnace (AMF).
prior_approach.evidence_span: Senkov et al. [ [36] ] reported that they succeeded in producing the refractory HEA WTaMoNbV considered in this research by using the conventional vacuum AMF.

prior_approach.content: Dobbelstein et al. were the first to produce the WTaMoNb alloy using direct deposition technology in 2016.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Dobbelstein et al. [ [12] ] were the first to produce this alloy with direct deposition technology in the form of a few consecutive layers in 2016.

prior_limitation.content: Prior approaches are limited by high production costs associated with using pre-alloyed powders from arc melting and gas atomization.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.

prior_limitation.content: Additive manufacturing efforts using a mix of elemental alloying powders yielded physical properties significantly inferior to those produced from pre-alloyed powders.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, the physical properties obtained in those studies were significantly inferior compared to AM samples produced from pre-alloyed powders.

prior_limitation.content: Prior work by Kang et al. is cited as an expectation regarding crystal structure, but the current text notes that the LPBF process introduces elemental distribution differences and defects not present in the AMF counterpart, implying a limitation of the LPBF process compared to the conventional method.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: as expected according to Kang et al. [ [48] ].

causal_claim.content: The presence of binding defects in primary LPBF trials is caused by inadequate fusion of consecutive powder layers.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Apparently, the relatively large amount of binding defects found in the primary LPBF trials can be related to inadequate fusion of consecutive powder layers

causal_claim.content: The observed peak shifts in LPBF samples are caused by normal residual stresses generated during additive manufacturing.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The shifting of these peaks can be related to normal residual stresses that are produced during the additive manufacturing process

causal_claim.content: The high density of dislocations observed is likely caused by internal stresses generated by the LPBF process.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Furthermore, evidence of high-density dislocations was also observed, and is probably due to common internal stresses inherently generated by the LPBF process

mechanism_principle.content: The binding defects are due to insufficient local energy density required for proper layer fusion.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This can be attributed to the insufficient local energy density that is required for proper layer fusion

mechanism_principle.content: The segregation of tungsten is due to its high melting temperature and high density compared to other elements.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This can be attributed mainly to the relatively high melting temperature and high density of W compared to other alloying elements

mechanism_principle.content: The depletion of W and increase of V at AMF grain boundaries is caused by the low melting temperature of V causing late solidification.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This phenomenon can be attributed to the relatively low melting temperature of V, which consequently solidified at the end of the solidification process, and hence was found to prefer grain boundaries

mechanism_principle.content: The higher compressive strength and brittleness of the LPBF alloy are related to microstructural differences, solidification defects, and finer grain size.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The higher compressive strength and more brittle fracture of the LPBF alloy may be related to differences in the microstructure and solidification defects and in the finer grain size

mechanism_principle.content: The difference in elemental distribution (vanadium at grain boundaries) is attributed to the disparity in melting temperatures between vanadium and tungsten.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This can mainly be related to the relatively low melting temperature of vanadium (1910 °C) versus tungsten (3422 °C), which consequently causes vanadium to solidify at grain boundaries during the final phase of the solidification process.

mechanism_principle.content: The increased number of small pits (defects) in the LPBF sample is attributed to non-homogeneous characteristics and inherent printing defects.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the small differences in the corrosion mechanism of the two alloys related to the relatively non-homogeneous characteristics of the LPBF sample and inherent printing defects.

mechanism_principle.content: The increased compressive strength of the LPBF sample is attributed to reduced grain size caused by rapid solidification.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The relatively increased compressive strength of the LPBF sample could be related to the relatively reduced grain size, due to inherent rapid solidification characteristics.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors propose that using spherical powders would improve flowability and homogeneity, representing a testable expectation for future optimization.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Hence it is believed that using spherical powders may improve the flowability of the powder and consequently increase homogeneity.

evidence_result.content: The average particle size of the elemental powders used ranges from 40 to 50 µm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the average particle size was between 40–50 µm

evidence_result.content: The LPBF samples exhibit significant defects like lack-of-fusion and porosity compared to the advanced trials and AMF counterpart.
evidence_result.evidence_span: This reveals a significant difference between the primary LPBF trials and the advanced LPBF trials in terms of inherent defects, mainly in the form of lack-of-fusion and porosity

evidence_result.content: Both LPBF and AMF alloys form a single solid phase solution with a BCC crystal structure.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Both alloys were composed of a single solid phase solution with a BCC crystal structure

evidence_result.content: W is found in high concentrations (37.6%) in bright grains while being depleted (15%) in neighboring areas.
evidence_result.evidence_span: This was manifested by a relatively high amount of W (37.6%) in bright grains shown in Area 1 compared to only 15% of W in a neighboring site (Area 2)

evidence_result.content: The AMF counterpart has a significantly larger average grain size (25 µm) compared to the LPBF samples (10 µm).
evidence_result.evidence_span: Although the counterpart alloy also presents a single solid phase solution structure, its grain size was significantly increased compared to the LPBF samples (average size 25 µm)

evidence_result.content: TEM analysis reveals the presence of sub-grains of about 500 nm size within the alloy matrix.
evidence_result.evidence_span: This high-resolution observation demonstrates the presence of sub-grains, with a size of about 500 nm, that compose the alloy matrix

evidence_result.content: Small precipitates (60–80 nm) with high V and low W content were dispersed along intergranular boundaries.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In addition, relatively small precipitates with a size of 60–80 nm and with a nearly spherical shape were dispersed along the intergranular boundaries

evidence_result.content: The LPBF sample density is 1.6% lower than the AMF sample.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The examined physical properties of HEa WTaMoNbV produced by the LPBF process were similar to those of the counterpart AMF alloy, being about 1.6% lower in terms of density

evidence_result.content: The LPBF sample has a higher ultimate compressive strength than the AMF sample.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The ultimate compressive strength of the LPBF sample was slightly higher than the counterpart AMF sample

constraint.content: The study identifies inherent printing defects as a limitation that requires additional experimental work and post-heat treatments to rectify, setting a boundary for the current process quality.
constraint.evidence_span: However, additional experimental work is required to further optimize the printing parameters to obtain improved properties and microstructure characteristics, mainly in terms of printing defects.
